html:
The Niger is West Africa's great river, about 4,200 km long. It rises in the Guinea highlands not far from the Atlantic, flows northeast to the edge of the Sahara, bends near Timbuktu, and runs southeast through Niger and Nigeria to a huge delta on the Gulf of Guinea.

In Mali it spreads into an inland delta that floods every year. There African rice was domesticated, and the city of Djenné-Djenno grew from about 250 BCE. Where the river meets the desert, gold and grain from the south met salt and camel caravans from the north, at Timbuktu and Gao. The empires of Mali and Songhai rose along it; Sonni Ali of Songhai used a river fleet to take Timbuktu and Djenné. Later the Bamana kingdom of Ségou ruled the middle river. Downstream, the Nok culture made its terracottas near the meeting of the Niger and the Benue.

Europeans long did not know where it ended; Mungo Park drowned on it in 1806, and the Lander brothers followed it to the sea in 1830. Then came the British Royal Niger Company on the lower river and the French Office du Niger irrigation scheme in Mali. Oil from its delta now pays much of Nigeria's way.
